title: Treen finishing and care
subtitle: Which finish to use on carved wooden pieces, and how to maintain them
excerpt: The right finish for a piece of treen depends on its use, a food-contact spoon, a decorative carving, and a garden tool handle all need different treatments. This guide covers the three finishes relevant to wood-craft projects in this category, how to apply them, when to re-apply, and what damages a finished wooden piece.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the linseed oil finishing protocol; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the board butter and wax finishing methods.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small wooden household objects made by hand carving, spoons, bowls, cups, ladles. From the Old English word for tree.
A wood finish that is safe for contact with food once fully cured. Raw linseed oil and board butter are food-safe; boiled linseed oil is not.
Cold-pressed linseed oil without additives. Food-safe after a two-week cure. Penetrates deeply into wood fibres and hardens over time.
Linseed oil treated with drying agents (metallic driers) to shorten cure time. NOT food-safe. Suitable for garden tools and outdoor woodwork.

content.text: Every carved wooden piece eventually needs a finish, and every finished piece eventually needs re-treatment. The finish choice is determined by use:
treen
that touches food takes a
food-safe finish
; outdoor woodwork takes boiled linseed oil. Getting this wrong, applying boiled linseed oil to a spoon, for example, is both a waste of wood and a potential health issue.
Raw linseed oil
The standard food-safe finish for carved kitchen woodware and food-contact pieces.
Raw linseed oil

is cold-pressed without metallic driers; it penetrates deeply and hardens by oxidation over two weeks. Application: pour a small amount onto the wood surface and work it in by hand, reaching all areas including end-grain. Leave for 30 minutes, then wipe off all excess oil, oil left on the surface remains tacky and attracts dirt. Cure time: two weeks at room temperature before using the piece for food contact. Re-apply when the wood starts to look dry (typically every 3, 6 months with regular use). Rags soaked in raw linseed oil must be laid flat to dry, never crumpled in a pile, which can build heat through oxidation.
Board butter

Board butter is a blend of mineral oil and beeswax or carnauba wax. Food-safe immediately after application. Application: apply generously to all surfaces by hand, leave for 10, 15 minutes to soak in, then buff off the excess with a cloth. The surface is immediately usable. Board butter is faster and simpler to apply than raw linseed oil and has no fire risk from rags. It does not penetrate as deeply as linseed oil, so it needs more frequent re-application (every 1, 2 months with heavy use). Best for cutting boards, food prep surfaces, and anyone who wants immediate food-safety without a two-week wait.
Boiled linseed oil
Boiled linseed oil

contains metallic driers (typically manganese or cobalt compounds) that shorten the cure time to 24, 48 hours. These driers make it unsuitable for food contact, it is not food-safe. Use BLO for: garden dibbers and rake handles, tool handles, green-woodwork pieces that will not contact food, and any outdoor wooden surface. Application: brush or wipe on, leave for 30 minutes, wipe off excess. BLO-soaked rags are a fire risk through spontaneous combustion, lay flat and allow to dry fully before disposal. Re-apply annually on outdoor pieces, or when the wood looks dry.
What damages finished wooden pieces
Soaking in water: do not leave wooden spoons or kuksas submerged in water. Rinse and dry promptly after use.
Dishwasher: heat and prolonged moisture will crack any carved wooden piece. Hand-wash only, dry immediately.
Direct heat: do not place wooden pieces directly next to a heat source or in direct sunlight for extended periods. Both accelerate checking and grain splitting.
Using BLO on food-contact items: the metallic driers are not safe to ingest. Keep BLO strictly for non-food items.
Signs a piece needs re-finishing
The wood looks pale or chalky rather than warm in colour.
The surface feels rough or dry to the touch.
Water no longer beads on the surface but is immediately absorbed.
